spec.title: Shared Lens workspace, project coordinators, chat and history

status.comment: Owner architecture requirements of 2026-09-15. This is the next product contract, not a claim that the paused prototype implements these features. Prototype-first delivery remains requested; exhaustive refinement is deferred.

p.product-boundary: org.vibevm.zap/lens owns one shared application server and platform-neutral client contracts. Quicklens is the browser/Electron presentation, Gamelens is the future game presentation, and Codlens includes the future VS Code and IntelliJ IDEA integrations as well as agent-facing integration assets. Multiple kinds of Lens may connect simultaneously. The separate org.vibevm.zap/zap engine remains authoritative for planning rules, economics, admission, plan versions and applied effects. The shared server coordinates services through public interfaces; it neither duplicates the planning engine nor depends on the host Vibevm source layout.

p.server-ownership: The shared server owns the project registry, project-scoped work contexts, managed agent sessions, dispatch queues, durable questions and answers, chat transcripts, event history, source watching and ZAP workflow composition. A renderer or an MCP connector does not instantiate a competing planning authority, workflow writer or source watcher for the same context. Thin local agent connectors and thin authenticated UI gateways call the shared application services. The existing durable broker and domain adapters are reused and consolidated rather than replaced solely to change presentation.

p.project-context: A project has a stable identity, display name and registered repository roots. Its work context identifies the exact checkout or worktree, branch/revision binding, planning store/campaign/base and coordinator conversation. Project, work context, actor, host session, conversation and client connection are distinct identities. A project has an explicit default work context; additional worktrees may have separate contexts. Every chat message, question, command and domain reference carries its exact project/context scope. Changing a client's selected project never changes another agent's working directory, context, authority or current plan.

p.project-views: Quicklens supports a focused project view and a board containing several selected projects. The board is a composition of separately scoped graph/read-model snapshots; it does not merge plans, invent cross-project dependencies or require a new global coordinator. Project identity remains visible on tasks, conversations, questions and history entries. Switching focus changes the user's view while other coordinators may continue. Cross-project commands or dependencies require an explicit supported operation rather than being inferred from visual proximity.

p.coordinator-lifecycle: A user can begin development from a Lens client by selecting a registered project/context and starting a background coordinator through a configured host adapter. The lifecycle distinguishes starting, bootstrapping, ready, running, waiting for user, stopped and failed. The initial agent is explicitly instructed that it is the project coordinator, receives the exact working context, and follows that project's complete applicable boot contract; it is not launched under a worker quiet clause. The server records the session and bootstrap boundary. Reopening a client, switching projects or sending another message resumes the registered conversation rather than creating another expensive coordinator. Loss of resumable context or changed boot inputs is explicit; no guarantee of provider prompt-cache reuse or exactly-once model reading is implied. The default coordinator host and automatic-versus-explicit start policy are configurable owner preferences.

p.workers: Each work context has one active coordinator binding by default, with many independently addressed workers or subagents. Independent contexts may run coordinators concurrently. Coordinator role is stated in the initial instruction and is separately enforced by scoped server capabilities; a model's role claim grants no authority. Delegated workers receive bounded task packets and their own actor identities according to the project's delegation rules. Workers may use the same question, message and artifact contracts without loading the coordinator's entire boot lane merely to communicate. The current implementation-worker preference remains native gpt-5.6-sol with high reasoning effort.

p.agent-adapters: Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode and Qwen Code implement one capability-described adapter seam for managed start, resume, user input, public output events, question/approval requests, interruption and exit. A Lens-managed background session and a user-started native session are distinct modes. Managed sessions use documented host server/SDK/structured process protocols. Native sessions may join through the existing broker integration without losing their ordinary text workflow. Connection to an arbitrary already-open CLI or desktop session, concurrent input, idle wake and native resume are claimed only where the actual adapter supports them. No terminal keystroke injection or transcript-file rewriting is used to simulate a universal adapter.

p.chat: A Lens client provides a durable conversation with the selected project coordinator, with user messages, public assistant responses, execution summaries and linked questions or plan changes. The server persists user input before dispatch and correlates host thread, turn and public item identities with its own stable messages. While a turn is running, new input is visibly queued or steered through a supported host operation; ordinary send never silently interrupts work. Interruption is an explicit action. Unsupported delivery remains visible and retriable according to its actual state. Persisted, queued, host-accepted, running, answered, failed and uncertain are distinct observations. The server does not start model turns to poll for updates or to render history. Hidden model reasoning is not a promised chat or history artifact.

p.rich-questions: A versioned structured question request supports a group of independently identified questions, short headers, explanatory Markdown, optional per-question context and artifact references, required/optional answers, single choice, multiple choice, short or multiline free text, an additional custom answer with choices, option labels/descriptions/previews and nonbinding recommendations. Typed number, date, boolean, project-object and file/image-reference inputs can extend the same contract without changing the transport. Validation, draft answers, submission, explicit skip where permitted, cancellation, expiry, clarification, answer amendment and earlier answer versions have explicit meanings. A recommended or preselected option is not a submitted answer. Stable question and option identities survive client presentation changes. This common schema must represent ordinary native agent questions without forcing the user back to a terminal; host-specific unsupported fields remain explicit rather than being silently discarded.

p.question-routing: The preferred agent-facing question action is ZapAskUserQuestion, displayed to the user as /ZapAskUserQuestion. Integration instructions supplied to coordinators and delegated workers direct ordinary user clarification questions through this action and require a short ordinary-text notice that the question was sent through /ZapAskUserQuestion. Concrete MCP tool naming or optional native slash-command aliases are host-adapter details, not a claim that every host has the same native command syntax. Publishing returns the durable question identity immediately. An agent may continue independent work; if progress requires an answer, its run becomes waiting for user without model polling. A reply resumes or steers the same addressed session through the adapter. Native user-question events may be mapped to this schema where interception is supported. Intrinsic host permission requests and exact ZAP Owner decisions retain their own authority and response contracts; a normal question answer cannot approve an unrelated action.

p.history: The shared server exposes a durable history independent of inbox completion: project/session lifecycle, public chat, question and answer changes, tool/execution lifecycle where observable, source-change signals, plan-rebuild requests, proposals, previews, holds, decisions, applied revisions and refusals. Every entry identifies its source, actor, project/context, occurrence and ingestion times, correlation/causation and source event identity where available. Native and ZAP events are ingested idempotently with durable cursors; original source ordering is retained. A server ingestion sequence orders the combined display without claiming a true global causal clock across independent projects. History coverage and gaps remain visible; events that were never captured are not fabricated. Credentials and hidden reasoning are not stored as ordinary history content.

p.plan-history: Plan-rebuild history links the request and its human or source-change cause to the public rationale, previous and proposed plan identities, exact source basis, affected tasks/milestones, approval or refusal and the actual applied revision. A proposal, decision and applied product remain distinct events. Historical views use an immutable snapshot or an exact revision read from ZAP; absence of such a snapshot is explicit. Inspecting an old plan does not activate it. Restoring historical intent is a new proposal through normal plan admission, not a rewrite of the event log. The inbox is the pending-action projection of this shared history, not its sole storage or user interface.

p.simultaneous-clients: All Lens clients use the same authoritative questions, chat, sessions and plans. Opening another client does not launch another coordinator or duplicate an answer delivery. Answer and command changes retain expected revisions and idempotency; multiple clients observe the committed winner and can explicitly amend where authorized. Current project selection, selected graph item, camera, presentation layout, theme and local drafts are client view state. Saved board definitions or user preferences may be synchronized explicitly without converting one window's focus into global project state.

p.shared-code: Keep maximum behavioral reuse in server services and platform-neutral protocol/client libraries: validation, history and conversation state, dispatch, question semantics, agent lifecycle and plan workflows are shared. Reusable Qwik components provide chat, inbox, history and cards where a client can host them. Quicklens and IDE webviews may share these components; Gamelens may present the same semantics differently. Sigma/Graphology coordinates and game-world layout remain presentation concerns. VS Code and IDEA native extensions are thin host bridges for project/file/editor integration and connection setup; they do not reimplement workflow authority or the full server. Logical modules remain inside org.vibevm.zap/lens for now, with explicit import/build boundaries suitable for later extraction.

p.network-boundary: The local agent/API channel and the password-authenticated HTTPS web gateway remain separate as specified in PROP-003. Internet clients call only named, authorized application actions for registered projects and configured agent profiles. A chat or agent-start action is not an arbitrary executable, shell command, working-directory or proxy endpoint. Agent processes, host protocol endpoints, credentials and ZAP controls remain behind the local server boundary. Launch/interrupt/chat permissions are scoped independently of viewing and answering questions; new UI capability does not enlarge an agent or Owner credential.

p.incremental-delivery: The next prototype first establishes the common server/project/context boundary and rich interaction/history contracts, then one managed coordinator adapter and a complete visible start-chat-question-answer-resume journey. It then adds project switching and a combined board using the same services, followed by the remaining host adapters and later Lens presentations. Work preserves the paused prototype and known integration gaps without claiming them complete. Verification stays proportionate to the current architecture: meaningful checks of project isolation, actor routing, startup duplication and the demonstrated interaction path plus applicable required build checks; no comparative model pilot, exhaustive host matrix or prolonged cosmetic/edge-case refinement before further owner architecture input.
